cur:manuscripts-valcavado-victory-of-the.summary: In a starry sky, the Lamb with a cross-staff stands triumphant above the beasts and the serpent, who lie defeated with their riders on a red ground below — 'the Lamb shall overcome them, for he is Lord of lords, and King of kings'.
facts: The Valcavado Beatus was written and illuminated in 970 by the monk Oveco for Abbot Sempronius of Valcavado, in the reign of Ramiro III of León; it has 230 surviving leaves and 87 miniatures.
After the expulsion of the Jesuits under Charles III, the manuscript passed from their college of San Ambrosio in Valladolid to the University of Valladolid.
cur:manuscripts-valcavado-victory-of-the.notes: Christ is represented as the Lamb.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-37-christ.summary: The psalmist, shown as a leper covered with sores and pierced by arrows, bends under a heavy sack laid on him by elf-like 'iniquities' and appeals to the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who has risen from his cushioned throne in a mandorla holding a bow and arrows. His friends stand afar off and his enemies whisper together. The drawing is one of the most moving images of suffering in the manuscript.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-37-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:objects-berlin-trier-moses-thomas-di.summary: On the left leaf Moses reaches up to receive the tablets of the Law from the hand of God; on the right the risen Christ, standing in a doorway, lifts his arm to reveal the wound in his side as Thomas reaches out to touch it. The two tall, slender figures in rich architectural frames set the Old Covenant beside the New. Christ's gesture offers the doubting apostle — and every viewer — tangible proof of the Resurrection.
facts: The Bode-Museum acquired the two leaves in 1935 (inv. nos. 8505/8506); they are attributed to Trier at the end of the 10th century, when Archbishop Egbert made the city a leading artistic centre.
Pairing Moses receiving the Law with Thomas touching Christ's wound sets the giving of the Old Law beside the revelation of the risen Lord (typological reading).

cur:objects-bm-raising-of-lazarus-ivory.summary: Christ strides forward with an apostle behind him, his hand extended toward the tomb, where Lazarus stands upright in his grave-clothes inside an arched niche; one of the sisters kneels at Christ's feet. Buildings of the town of Bethany rise in the background. The slim panel captures the instant of Christ's command, 'Lazarus, come forth'.
facts: The British Museum catalogues the plaque as Byzantine Empire or Italy (Venice?), about 900–1000, showing that the attribution of such ivories between Byzantium and its Italian imitators can be difficult.

cur:objects-golden-altar-sant-ambrogio.summary: At the centre of the golden front of the high altar Christ is enthroned in a cross-shaped frame, surrounded by the symbols of the evangelists and the twelve apostles; panels on either side narrate the life of Christ, from the Annunciation and Nativity to miracles, the Crucifixion, Resurrection and Ascension. Gems and enamels set into filigree frames make the altar a shining reliquary-like casing. It is one of the supreme achievements of Carolingian goldsmiths' work, still in use over the relics of St Ambrose.
facts: Italian Wikipedia notes that it was made between 824 and 859 for Bishop Angilbert II and is signed by 'Vuolvino magister phaber' (Wolvinius), hence also called the Altar of Volvinio.
It stands over the relics of Saints Gervasius, Protasius and Ambrose, which can still be seen through a small window from the crypt.

Q5113613.summary: The risen Christ stands above the altar of Copenhagen Cathedral with open, lowered arms and a gently bowed head, showing the wounds in his hands as he welcomes all who approach. According to his biographer, Thorvaldsen, the leading Neoclassical sculptor of his age, lowered the heavenward-raised arms of an earlier model into a gesture of quiet invitation, creating what became one of the most reproduced images of Christ in the world.
facts: The pedestal bears the words "Kommer til mig" ("Come unto me") from Matthew 11:28, which give the statue its meaning.

The work was largely carried out in Thorvaldsen's workshops in Rome, where he spent most of his career; the statue anchors a cycle of the apostles made for the rebuilt cathedral, with St Paul taking the place of Judas.
Full-size and reduced copies stand around the world, most famously in the visitors' centres of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, including Temple Square in Salt Lake City.
The original plaster model is preserved in the Thorvaldsens Museum in Copenhagen.

Q7751053.summary: A kneeling knight in armour prays before a wayside shrine, and the carved wooden Christ leans down from his cross to embrace and kiss him. The scene illustrates the legend of a Florentine knight, Saint John Gualbert, who on Good Friday spared the life of his brother's murderer and was blessed by the crucifix for his mercy. Burne-Jones wraps the miracle in a dense, jewel-like garden of flowers.
facts: Burne-Jones knew the legend from Kenelm Digby's chivalric book The Broad Stone of Honour, a favourite of Victorian medievalists.

It is often called Burne-Jones's most important early work, and it remained his own favourite among his early pictures; the marigolds in the foreground are said to have come from a garden in Russell Square near his London home.
Burne-Jones was born in Birmingham, and the city's museum now holds one of the largest collections of his work.
